analysis.one_liner: Bans the manufacture, use, and sale of asbestos, with a two-year phase-out for chlorine plants.
analysis.headline: The asbestos ban bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in May 2022 and never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would ban companies from making, using, or selling commercial asbestos, or products containing it, one year after enactment. Chlorine plants that use asbestos equipment would get two extra years to switch, and the President could grant national-security exemptions. Companies that handle asbestos would also have to report their use and exposure estimates to the EPA, which would publish the information.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and the public who are exposed to asbestos on the job and in buildings. Asbestos causes mesothelioma, lung cancer, and other fatal diseases, often decades after exposure, so a ban prevents future cases among factory workers, construction workers, and people living and working in buildings with asbestos products. The bill would also give the public access to company-by-company data on who is using asbestos and how many people are exposed.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and the public exposed to asbestos

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the manufacture, processing, use, and distribution in commerce of commercial asbestos and any mixture or article containing it, effective one year after enactment.

Requires any company that handled asbestos in the previous three years, or during the phase-out period, to report to the EPA where it used asbestos, in what quantities, and its estimates of how many people were exposed; those reports must be made public.
Directs the EPA to publicize the ban and help companies comply with it.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that manufacture, import, or use asbestos. The main cost falls on chlor-alkali plants (which make chlorine and caustic soda) that still use asbestos-based equipment: they get a two-year window to keep importing asbestos, then must pay to convert to asbestos-free technology, and those conversion costs would flow into prices for chlorine-based products. Building owners and demolition contractors also face established disposal rules for asbestos already in place, though the bill does not change those.

drawbacks.text: The bill carves out asbestos present solely as an 'impurity' and states it has no effect on how cosmetics are regulated, so talc-based cosmetics and other products with trace asbestos would remain outside the ban.
Chlor-alkali plants would get two more years to import and process asbestos for equipment, extending worker exposure at those facilities while they convert.
The President could grant national-security exemptions of up to three years, extendable once for another three, and could withhold publication of exemption details on security grounds.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health benefit is large and permanent: asbestos has no safe exposure level, and the people most exposed are industrial and construction workers. The costs are concentrated and transitional — mainly a handful of chlorine plants converting to asbestos-free equipment during a grace period the bill itself provides. The main design weakness is that the impurity and cosmetics exclusions leave trace-asbestos products, including some talc-based cosmetics, untouched, and the national-security exemption is broad and potentially renewable for six years.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Bonamici introduced the bill on May 18, 2022, with five Democratic cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed, and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Asbestos importers and the chlorine plants that still use asbestos equipment are better off, since the ban never took effect and they continue operating under existing rules. People exposed to asbestos at work and in buildings gained nothing from the bill's death.

for.name: Rep. Suzanne Bonamici
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor.

for.name: Asbestos Disease Awareness Organization
for.role: Victim and public health advocacy group
for.what_they_did: Championed legislation named for Alan Reinstein, who died of mesothelioma, and pushed for a full asbestos ban.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — leaving the bill to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Chlor-alkali industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed full asbestos bans and sought long lead times to convert plants, having won a gradual transition in prior versions of the legislation.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill's sponsor and all five cosponsors were House Democrats, so its level of support in both parties was never tested.

industries.note: A small number of plants that make chlorine and caustic soda still use asbestos-based diaphragms; the bill gives them two years to keep importing asbestos, then forces a switch to asbestos-free technology, with conversion costs passed into product prices. Their interest in continuing asbestos use runs directly against the public's interest in ending exposure.

industries.industry: Asbestos importers and asbestos-containing product makers
industries.note: The bill ends their market for raw asbestos and asbestos-containing products one year after enactment and imposes detailed public reporting on their use and exposures.

The bill explicitly excludes asbestos present only as an impurity and leaves cosmetic regulation untouched, so products with trace asbestos would not be affected. This carve-out preserves the status quo for an industry that has faced asbestos-contamination concerns.
